To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Caffeine reduces the coupling ratio, and increases baseline metabolism and blood flow in the human brain.

the effects of caffeine in humans on baseline blood flow and oxygenation level dependent signal and on the coupling ratio of the evoked blood flow and oxygen consumption responses to a visual stimulus are opposite in direction, resulting in similar BOLD responses to a visual stimulation before and after caffeine administration despite large changes in underlying physiological parameters.

caffeine administration in humans leads to an increase in the coupling ratio, and a decrease in the baseline blood oxygenation level, both of which reduce the subsequent BOLD signal to a visual stimulus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the physiological mechanisms of the fMRI BOLD signal.
the development of a quantitative functional magnetic resonance imaging (qMRI) technique for measuring brain function.
the development and use of a quantitative approach to fMRI.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the magnitude of BOLD response is not a direct measure of neural activity, and the quantitative methodology based on simultaneous measurement of blood flow, oxygen metabolism and BOLD responses would be more promising tool for applying the fMRI to disease or drug studies in which baseline conditions and the relationship of blood flow and metabolism responses to a stimuli are altered.
this study has shown that caffeine administration in humans has the potential to alter baseline oxygen metabolism and evoked oxygen metabolism responses to visual stimulation.

caffeine administration in humans leads to a decrease in the coupling of the evoked blood flow and oxygen metabolic responses to a stimulus, and that this decrease in the coupling ratio is sufficient to compensate for the large physiological changes in the underlying baseline state.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how quantitative fMRI can be applied to a pharmacological study and how this approach can be used to understand the underlying mechanisms of the BOLD signal.
the quantitative fMRI approach provides an opportunity to study the effects of drugs and diseases on brain physiology in a manner not possible with traditional BOLD fMRI.

the magnitude of BOLD response alone cannot be interpreted as a measure of the underlying neurophysiological change, but a dual-echo measurement method based on quantitative fMRI can be used to investigate the effects of caffeine in healthy human subjects and to investigate the effects on disease and drugs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the magnitude of BOLD response alone cannot be used to infer changes in underlying neurophysiological processes.

fMRI is a promising tool that can provide quantitative measures of neurophysiology, but the BOLD signal alone should not be used to interpret the magnitude of neurophysiological changes in disease and drug studies.

the BOLD response to visual stimuli is not directly related to neural activation and that the interpretation of BOLD responses requires a quantitative approach that accounts for the effects of physiological factors.
